# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review: Varden County 30-Hour Week Trial (Nine-Month Results)

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It fixes most of the problems I raised there:
- offices were randomised and stratified by type of work;
- output comes from administrative records, not manager judgement;
- actual hours come from timesheets, not schedules;
- the protocol and analysis plan were registered;
- the exploratory meetings analysis is clearly labelled as such.

Its conclusions are mostly measured. The problems below are real, but they are about refinement, not about the main result.

## Arithmetic check

Everything I could recompute is consistent:

| Claim | Check |
|---|---|
| Actual hours −13% (case-processing) | 33.0 / 37.9 = 0.871 ✓ |
| Actual hours −17% (counter) | 31.2 / 37.6 = 0.830 ✓ |
| Output per actual hour +12.5% (case) | 0.979 / 0.87 = 1.125 ✓ |
| Output per actual hour +6.7% (counter) | 0.886 / 0.83 = 1.067 ✓ |
| "Would appear as 22%" against scheduled hours | 0.979 / 0.80 = 1.224 ✓ |
| Confidence intervals | Asymmetric where expected (log scale); widths plausible ✓ |

## 1. The meetings arithmetic suggests meetings may explain *most* of the case-processing gain, not "part"

The authors' own numbers support a stronger statement than they make. Subtract meeting time from actual hours:

- **Control:** 37.9 − 7.1 = 30.8 non-meeting hours per week. This assumes control hours stayed near the case-processing pre-period level, which the paper says they did.
- **Treated:** 33.0 − 3.8 = 29.2 non-meeting hours per week.

So non-meeting working time fell only about 5%, while output fell 2.1%. Output per non-meeting hour rose about **3%**, against **12.5%** per total hour.

If the meetings difference was caused by the treatment, cutting meetings accounts for roughly three-quarters of the per-hour gain. That leaves little room for the rest-and-fatigue explanation.

That is a big "if," and the authors' caution is right:
- the meetings data come from month six only, with no pre-period, so the 3.3-hour gap is a cross-section and not a difference-in-differences estimate;
- r = 0.71 across seven offices has a 95% CI running from roughly zero to about 0.95;
- managers who cut meetings may simply be more effective managers.

Even so, the summary's "may account for part of the gain" undersells what the data suggest. It is worth stating this calculation in the paper and pre-registering it for the 24-month follow-up, ideally with pre-period calendar data.

## 2. In counter work, "output per hour" is mostly busier staff, not more productive staff

In a queue-driven service, the work that arrives is set by the public, not by staff. When fewer staff serve the same queue, each is idle less, so contacts per staff hour rise automatically. The cost shows up in waiting times, which is exactly what the paper observes.

So the +6.7% "productivity gain" in counter offices is largely a utilisation effect. Presenting it next to the case-processing +12.5% as if the two were alike is misleading. The Discussion's line that "each hour worked was somewhat more productive" should be reframed around queueing: the same people did less waiting between customers, and the public did more waiting instead.

A related puzzle: contacts handled fell 11.4%, but call abandonment rose only from 6% to 10%. That explains only about 4 points of the fall. The paper should say where the rest of the demand went. Possibilities include:
- in-person visitors who left without being counted;
- people shifting to online channels;
- people going to *control* offices (see section 5).

Repeat contacts also rose (11.8% v 10.9%). Repeat contacts count as output, so the real fall in service is slightly larger than 11.4%.

## 3. Sick days may fall mechanically

If 30 hours is delivered as four 7.5-hour days, staff have about 20% fewer scheduled working days. Sickness counted in days per employee would then fall by about 20% even if people were ill exactly as often. The paper doesn't say how rotas were arranged.

That could explain most of the 29% fall. Sickness should be reported as a rate per scheduled day or per scheduled hour. The −29% figure also has no confidence interval, unlike the other outcomes.

## 4. The cost of the reform is missing, and overtime drives it

Case-processing offices went from about 0.4 to about 3 hours of overtime per week per employee (actual 33.0 against 30 scheduled). If overtime is paid at a premium on top of unchanged base pay, cost per case rose substantially. At time-and-a-half, it could be on the order of 10–15% of the wage bill.

The county's stated question was whether the change could be made "without loss of service." Cost is part of that question. Report:
- overtime cost;
- cost per case;
- backlog size and age against statutory deadlines.

On the last point: output per employee is 2.1% lower, and the limitations already flag the risk of backlogs building past deadlines. Backlog is measurable now, so it should be measured now rather than left to the follow-up. A check for case-mix shifting (closing easier cases first) would also help.

## 5. Inference with very few clusters

Cluster-robust standard errors are biased downward with 7 v 7 clusters, and badly so with 5 v 5. The CIs reported, especially for the counter stratum, are probably too narrow.

Re-estimate using one of:
- a wild cluster bootstrap;
- randomisation inference (permutation tests);
- a small-sample correction such as CR2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

The counter-stratum output loss is large enough that it will probably survive, but the per-hour CI of +0.4 to +13.3 may not.

## 6. Gaps between the design and what is reported

- **Primary outcome.** The registered primary outcome is output per FTE, but no pooled estimate is reported. Was the stratum-specific analysis the registered primary analysis? If not, say so and report the pooled estimate.
- **Difference between strata.** The paper's central contrast is between the two strata, yet there is no formal test of that difference (an interaction test). Add one.
- **Missing comparisons.** Some outcomes have no comparison with control offices:
  - waiting time (4.2 → 6.9 minutes) is a before–after figure for treated offices only;
  - abandoned calls (6% → 10%) likewise, and it isn't in the table;
  - the quality figures (3.1% v 3.0%, 11.8% v 10.9%) don't say whether they are treated versus control or differences-in-differences, and they have no CIs.

  All of these are registered secondary outcomes and should get the same difference-in-differences treatment as the rest.
- **Resignations.** 3.9% v 7.4% compares levels, not differences-in-differences, and the event count isn't given.
- **"FTE."** If FTE is rebased to contracted hours, a 30-hour employee becomes 0.8 FTE and every per-FTE number changes. The summary says "per full-time employee," so it probably means per head. State this explicitly.

## 7. Spillovers between offices

Randomising by office avoids contamination between colleagues, but these offices belong to one county government, so the arms may not be independent. If treated counter offices got slower, some of the public may have switched to control offices or to online channels. That would raise control output and make the treatment effect look worse than it is, or it may explain the missing demand in section 2.

Morale effects are also possible: control staff knew about the trial, so resentment or extra effort to keep up could have shifted their results. The limitations mention awareness of the trial but not demand moving between offices. Check whether control offices' volumes changed.

## Smaller points

- In the summary, "a more modest 6.7%" sits next to the 12.5% without warning that the two measure different things (see section 2).
- Third Discussion conclusion: the scheduled-versus-actual overstatement is measured, but it applies to case-processing only. The counter figure would be +10.8% against scheduled hours versus +6.7% against actual hours. Give both.
- The line "These findings qualify claims… that reduced hours are sector-general" is well judged. Defining the boundary by the role rather than the sector is the paper's most useful general point.

## Bottom line

The registered findings are credible and well presented:
- a 20% cut in schedule became a 13–17% cut in actual hours;
- output per head was roughly maintained in backlog work and fell by about a tenth in presence-bound work, where the public waited noticeably longer;
- per-hour figures based on scheduled hours are inflated.

The improvements that matter most:
- fix the small-cluster inference;
- give counter outcomes the same difference-in-differences and CI treatment;
- check whether the sick-day fall is mechanical;
- report cost and backlog;
- reframe the counter per-hour "gain" as a utilisation effect.

The exploratory meetings result, if it holds, is more important than the authors suggest. It would mean much of the benefit could be had without cutting hours at all.
